assignments.description:
In the Monty Hall problem, you’re on a game show with 3 doors:

  • Behind 1 door: a car (win!) 🚗

  • Behind the other 2 doors: goats 🐐🐐

You pick a door.
The host (who knows where the car is) then opens one of the other two doors, always showing a goat.

Now you’re given a choice:

  • Stay with your original door

  • Switch to the other unopened door

What should you do?

assignments.description:
For your first assignment, do an internet search for something like, "online Python code compiler" unless you have an environment you like better.

Please email me at [redacted-instructor-email] if you need anything or if something happens that is unexpected. Or you can text me at [redacted-instructor-phone]. 

Use an online tool if you would like to complete this assignment. 

You will need to copy your code and results into a document. Add a little discussion. Upload document to discussion on Canvas for credit.

Link to example of what the homework could look like from 2024 with links to install Visual Studio Code and directions to connect GitHub Copilot: [redacted-external-doc-link]

Video to help you get started: https://youtu.be/qSMzAtYngeA

Video on how to install software on a Windows computer (PC): https://youtu.be/cd0I_xvPFvk

Note that the video does discuss Mac, Linux, and Chrome Book

Grading Structure:

Please do 3 problems from this week’s Chapter. You may substitute a problem of your own creation based on that week’s chapter. 

Base Points: Criteria (not stacking)
25 points: Demonstration of effort, but no working codes
50 points: Have one programming solution working
75 points: Have two programming solutions working
100 points: Have three programming solutions working
    Bonus: (Stacking)
10 points: Some improvement on one problem.
20 points: Some improvement on two problems.
30 points: All three programming solutions work with some improvement on three problems.
25 points: You record a video and talk about how or why you worked your problems the way you did
50 points: Push your code to the SWOSU shared repository and post your link: https://github.com/swosu/SwosuCsPythonExamples/tree/main/Student_Codes
You will need to post your link in the discussion to receive bonus points for this.
25 points: Anyone who presents during class.

1.15 LAB: Formatted output: Hello World!

Welcome to zyBooks!

Mad Libs are activities that have a person provide various words, which are then used to complete a short story in unexpected (and hopefully funny) ways.

Complete a program that reads four values from input and stores the values in variables first_name, generic_location, whole_number, and plural_noun. The program then uses the input values to output a short story. The first input statement is provided in the code as an example.

Notes: To test your program in the Develop mode, pre-enter four values (in separate lines) in the input box and click the Run program button. The auto-grader in the Submit mode will test your program with different sets input of values.

Eric
12
cars
Chipotle

then the program uses the input values and outputs a story:

Eric buys 12 different types of cars at Chipotle

Ex: If the input values are:

Brenda
6
bells
Phillys

then the program uses the input values and outputs a story:

Brenda buys 6 different types of bells at Phillys


 


 


Bonus: 


100 Points for People's Choice Best MadLib


50 points for the longest code


25 points for the "you tried" self-nominated category.

The program contains syntax and logic errors. Fix the syntax errors in the Develop mode until the program executes. Then fix the logic errors.

One error often causes additional errors further along in the program. For this exercise, fix the first error reported. Then try to run the program again. Repeat until all the syntax errors have been corrected.


The correct output of the program is:


Is Pluto a planet?
Some people think so, but others don't.
The Moon's mass is 6 times Pluto's.
Not much of a planet, is it?

18.5 LAB*: Program: Phone directory












Program Specifications Write a program to input a phone number and output a phone directory with five international numbers. Phone numbers are divided into four parts: 1) country code, 2) area code, 3) prefix, and 4) line number. For example, a phone number in the United States is +1 (555) 123-4567.

Note: this program is designed for incremental development. Complete each step and submit for grading before starting the next step. Only a portion of tests pass after each step but confirm progress.

Step 1 (2 pts). Read from input an area code, prefix, and line number (integers). Output the directory heading (two lines). Insert two blank spaces between Country and Phone and the horizontal line is created with dashes (not underscores). Output a phone number for the United States with country code +1 using proper format. Submit for grading to confirm 2 tests pass.
Ex: If the input is:


555  457  2345



The output is:


Country  Phone Number
-------  ------------
U.S.     +1 (555)457-2345



Step 2 (2 pts). Output a phone number for Brazil with country code +55 and add 100 to the prefix. The prefix variable should not change. Instead, add 100 to the prefix within the print statement. For example, print(f"){prefixNum + 100}-"). Submit for grading to confirm 3 tests pass.
Ex: If the input is:


555  457  2345



The output is:


Country  Phone Number
-------  ------------
U.S.     +1 (555)457-2345
Brazil   +55 (555)557-2345



Step 3 (2 pts). Output a phone number for Croatia with country code +385 and add 50 to the line number. Output a phone number for Egypt with country code +20 and add 30 to the area code. The variables should not change. Instead, add values within the print statement as in Step 2. Submit for grading to confirm 4 tests pass.
Ex: If the input is:


555  929  6453



The output is:


Country  Phone Number
-------  ------------
U.S.     +1 (555)929-6453
Brazil   +55 (555)1029-6453
Croatia  +385 (555)929-6503
Egypt    +20 (585)929-6453



Step 4 (2 pts). Output a phone number for France with country code +33 and swap the area code with the prefix. Submit for grading to confirm all tests pass.
Ex: If the input is:


555  929  6453



The output is:


Country  Phone Number
-------  ------------
U.S.     +1 (555)929-6453
Brazil   +55 (555)1029-6453
Croatia  +385 (555)929-6503
Egypt    +20 (585)929-6453
France   +33 (929)555-6453

Suggested Problems:

# Problem:

2.13 LAB: Divide input integers

Write a program that reads integers user_num and div_num as input, and outputs user_num divided by div_num three times using floor divisions.

Ex: If the input is:

2000
2

the output is:

1000 500 250

Note: In Python 3, floor division discards fractions. Ex: 6 // 4 is 1 (the 0.5 is discarded).

# Problem:

2.14 LAB: Driving costs

Driving is expensive. Write a program with a car's gas mileage (miles/gallon) and the cost of gas (dollars/gallon) as floating-point input, and output the gas cost for 20 miles, 75 miles, and 500 miles.

Output each floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print(f'{your_value1:.2f} {your_value2:.2f} {your_value3:.2f}')

Ex: If the input is:

25.0
3.1599

where the gas mileage is 25.0 miles/gallon and the cost of gas is $3.1599/gallon, the output is:

2.53 9.48 63.20

Note: Real per-mile cost would also include maintenance and depreciation.

# Problem:

2.15 LAB: Expression for calories burned during workout

LAB ACTIVITY
2.15.1: LAB: Expression for calories burned during workout
open_in_newfullscreen0 / 10

The following equation estimates the average calories burned for a person when exercising, which is based on a scientific journal article (source):

 

starter code:

''' Calories = ((Age x 0.2757) + (Weight x 0.03295) + (Heart Rate x 1.0781) — 75.4991) x Time / 8.368 '''

 

Write a program using inputs age (years), weight (pounds), heart rate (beats per minute), and time (minutes), respectively. Output the average calories burned for a person.

Output each floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print(f'Calories: {calories:.2f} calories')

Ex: If the input is:

49
155
148
60

then the output is:

Calories: 736.21 calories

2.16 LAB: Using math functions

Given three floating-point numbers x, y, and z, output x to the power of z, x to the power of (y to the power of z), the absolute value of (x minus y), and the square root of (x to the power of z).

Output each floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print(f'{your_value1:.2f} {your_value2:.2f} {your_value3:.2f} {your_value4:.2f}')

Ex: If the input is:

5.0
1.5
3.2

Then the output is:

172.47 361.66 3.50 13.13

# Problem:

Please do 3 problems from this week’s Chapter. You may substitute a problem of your own creation based on that week’s chapter. 

Base Points: Criteria (not stacking)

    Bonus: (Stacking)
10 points: Some improvement on one problem.

50 points: Push your code to the SWOSU shared repository and post your link: https://github.com/swosu/SwosuCsPythonExamples/tree/main/Student_Codes
You will need to post your link in the discussion to receive bonus points for this.
25 points: Anyone that presents during class.

Program Specifications. Write a program to calculate the cost of hosting three pizza parties on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Read from input the number of people attending, the average number of slices per person and the cost of one pizza. Dollar values are output with two decimals. For example, print(f"Cost: ${cost:.2f}").

Note: this program is designed for incremental development. Complete each step and submit for grading before starting the next step. Only a portion of tests pass after each step but confirm progress.


Step 1 (2 pts). Read from input the number of people (int), average slices per person (float) and cost of one pizza (float). Calculate the number of whole pizzas needed (8 slices per pizza). There will likely be leftovers for breakfast. Hint: Use the ceil() function from the math library to round up to the nearest whole number and convert to an int. Calculate and output the cost for all pizzas. Submit for grading to confirm test 1 passes.
Ex: If the input is:


10  2.6  10.50



The output is:


Friday Night Party
4 Pizzas: $42.00




Step 2 (2 pts). Calculate and output the sales tax (7%). Calculate and output the delivery charge (20% of cost including tax). Submit for grading to confirm 2 tests pass.
Ex: If the input is:


10  2.6  10.50



The output is:


Friday Night Party
4 Pizzas: $42.00
Tax: $2.94
Delivery: $8.99




Step 3 (2 pts). Calculate and output the total including pizza, tax and delivery. Submit for grading to confirm 3 tests pass.
Ex: If the input is:


10  2.6  10.50



The output is:


Friday Night Party
4 Pizzas: $42.00
Tax: $2.94
Delivery: $8.99
Total: $53.93




Step 4 (2 pts). Repeat steps 1 - 3 with additional inputs for Saturday night (one order per line). Maintain and output a separate total for both parties. Submit for grading to confirm 5 tests pass.
Ex: If the input is:


9   2.5   10.95
14   3.2   14.95



The output is:


Friday Night Party
3 Pizzas: $32.85
Tax: $2.30
Delivery: $7.03
Total: $42.18

Saturday Night Party

Tax: $6.28
Delivery: $19.20
Total: $115.17

Weekend Total: $157.35

6   2.8   10.95

# Problem : )

4.15 LAB: Interstate highway numbers

Primary U.S. interstate highways are numbered 1-99. Odd numbers (like the 5 or 95) go north/south, and evens (like the 10 or 90) go east/west. Auxiliary highways are numbered 100-999, and service the primary highway indicated by the rightmost two digits. Thus, I-405 services I-5, and I-290 services I-90. Note: 200 is not a valid auxiliary highway because 00 is not a valid primary highway number.

Given a highway number, indicate whether it is a primary or auxiliary highway. If auxiliary, indicate what primary highway it serves. Also indicate if the (primary) highway runs north/south or east/west.

Ex: If the input is:

90

the output is:

I-90 is primary, going east/west.

Ex: If the input is:

290

the output is:

I-290 is auxiliary, serving I-90, going east/west.

Ex: If the input is:

0

the output is:

0 is not a valid interstate highway number.

Ex: If the input is:

200

the output is:

200 is not a valid interstate highway number.

See Wikipedia for more info on highway numbering.

# Coding Odyssey 1

**Instructor: Jeremy Evert**  
**Contact: Email - [redacted-instructor-email] | Text - [redacted-instructor-phone]**  

## Objective:
This assignment aims to encourage you to apply the programming concepts and tools you have learned in class to build a project of your choice. The goal is to foster creativity, problem-solving, and practical application of theoretical knowledge.

## Assignment Guidelines:

1. **Project Selection**:
   - Choose a project idea that interests you. It can be a game, a utility, a simulation, or any other application.
   - Ensure that your project incorporates most of the concepts we have covered in class, including but not limited to:
     - Variables and Data Types
     - Control Structures (loops, conditionals)
     - Functions and Modular Programming
     - Basic Data Structures (lists, dictionaries)
     - File I/O
     - Error Handling
     - (Optional) Basic GUI elements (if you wish to explore)

2. **Design Phase**:
   - **Design Document**: Create a design document outlining the following:
     - **Project Title**: Name of your project.
     - **Description**: A brief overview of what your project does.
     - **Features**: List the main features of your project.
     - **Tools/Technologies**: Identify the tools, libraries, and languages you will use.
     - **Flowchart/Diagram**: Provide a flowchart or diagram of your program’s architecture.
     - **Milestones**: Break down your project into smaller tasks or milestones.

3. **Implementation Phase**:
   - Start coding your project based on your design document.
   - Ensure that you write clean, readable, and well-documented code.
   - Use version control (e.g., Git) to track your progress and changes.

4. **Testing and Debugging**:
   - Test your code regularly to catch and fix bugs early.
   - Ensure that your code handles errors gracefully and includes appropriate error messages.

5. **Final Submission**:
   - Submit the following:
     - **Design Document**: Updated if there were any changes during implementation.
     - **Source Code**: All the code files of your project.
     - **Readme File**: Instructions on how to run your project, any dependencies, and a brief user guide.
     - **Demonstration**: (Optional) A short video or presentation demonstrating your project.

## Grading Structure:

- **Base Points (Not Stacking)**:
  - **25 Points**: You have a design for your idea.
  - **50 Points**: You have a design and some code.
  - **75 Points**: You have a design and some of your code runs.
  - **100 Points**: You have a design and a working code.

- **Bonus Points**:
  - **Creativity**: Innovative and original ideas.
  - **Efficiency**: Optimal use of resources and efficient algorithms.
  - **Enjoyment**: Fun and engaging user experience.
  - **Clean Code**: Well-structured, commented, and readable code.

## Submission:
- Submit your project through the course’s submission portal or email it directly to [redacted-instructor-email] by the due date.

## Tips for Success:
- **Plan Ahead**: Start with a clear plan and follow it.
- **Stay Organized**: Keep your code and resources well-organized.
- **Seek Help**: If you encounter any issues, feel free to reach out for help.
- **Experiment and Learn**: Don’t be afraid to try new things and learn from them.

Good luck, and happy coding!

---

6.18 Lab training: Unit tests to evaluate your program

Auto-graded programming assignments may use a Unit test to test small parts of a program. Unlike a Compare output test, which evaluates your program's output for specific input values, a Unit test evaluates individual functions to determines if each function:

  • is named correctly and has the correct parameters and return type
  • calculates and returns the correct value (or prints the correct output)

The zyLabs auto-grader runs main.py as a script. In main.py, the line if __name__ == '__main__': is used to separate the main code from the functions' code so that each function can be unit tested. Enter statements to be run as the main code under if __name__ == '__main__':. Indent the statements so the statements belong to the if block. Refer to the subsection Importing modules and executing scripts under section Module basics for more information about running a program as a script.

Note: Do not remove if __name__ == '__main__': from the code. Otherwise, the unit tests will fail even though the program produces the correct output.

This example lab uses multiple unit tests to test the kilo_to_pounds() function.

Complete a program that takes a weight in kilograms as input, converts the weight to pounds, and then outputs the weight in pounds. 1 kilogram = 2.204 pounds (lbs).

The program must define the following function:
def kilo_to_pounds(kilos) - take kilos as a parameter, convert kilos from kilograms to pounds, and return the weight in pounds.

Ex: If the input of the program is:

10

22.040 lbs

The program below has an error in the kilo_to_pounds() function.

The first test case fails because the program outputs the result from the kilo_to_pounds() function, which has an error. The second test case uses a Unit test to test the kilo_to_pounds() function, which fails.

  2. Change the kilo_to_pounds() function to multiply the variable kilos by 2.204, instead of dividing. The return statement should be: return (kilos * 2.204). Submit again. Now the test cases should all pass.

Note: A common error is to mistype a function name with the incorrect capitalization. Function names are case sensitive, so if a lab program asks for a kilo_to_pounds() function, a kilo_To_Pounds() function that works for you in "Develop mode" will result in a failed unit test. The unit test will not be able to find kilo_to_pounds().

6.18 Lab training: Unit tests to evaluate your program

Auto-graded programming assignments may use a Unit test to test small parts of a program. Unlike a Compare output test, which evaluates your program's output for specific input values, a Unit test evaluates individual functions to determines if each function:

  • is named correctly and has the correct parameters and return type
  • calculates and returns the correct value (or prints the correct output)

The zyLabs auto-grader runs main.py as a script. In main.py, the line if __name__ == '__main__': is used to separate the main code from the functions' code so that each function can be unit tested. Enter statements to be run as the main code under if __name__ == '__main__':. Indent the statements so the statements belong to the if block. Refer to the subsection Importing modules and executing scripts under section Module basics for more information about running a program as a script.

Note: Do not remove if __name__ == '__main__': from the code. Otherwise, the unit tests will fail even though the program produces the correct output.

This example lab uses multiple unit tests to test the kilo_to_pounds() function.

Complete a program that takes a weight in kilograms as input, converts the weight to pounds, and then outputs the weight in pounds. 1 kilogram = 2.204 pounds (lbs).

The program must define the following function:
def kilo_to_pounds(kilos) - take kilos as a parameter, convert kilos from kilograms to pounds, and return the weight in pounds.

Ex: If the input of the program is:

The first test case fails because the program outputs the result from the kilo_to_pounds() function, which has an error. The second test case uses a Unit test to test the kilo_to_pounds() function, which fails.

  2. Change the kilo_to_pounds() function to multiply the variable kilos by 2.204, instead of dividing. The return statement should be: return (kilos * 2.204). Submit again. Now the test cases should all pass.

Note: A common error is to mistype a function name with the incorrect capitalization. Function names are case sensitive, so if a lab program asks for a kilo_to_pounds() function, a kilo_To_Pounds() function that works for you in "Develop mode" will result in a failed unit test. # Problem : ) 

9.11 LAB: Car value (classes)

Complete the Car class by creating an attribute purchase_price (type int) and the method print_info() that outputs the car's information.

Ex: If the input is:

2011
18000
2018

where 2011 is the car's model year, 18000 is the purchase price, and 2018 is the current year, then print_info() outputs:

Car's information:
  Model year: 2011
  Purchase price: $18000
  Current value: $5770

Note: print_info() should use two spaces for indentation.

# Starter Code :

class Car:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model_year = 0
        # TODO: Declare purchase_price attribute
      
        self.current_value = 0

    def calc_current_value(self, current_year):
        depreciation_rate = 0.15
        # Car depreciation formula
        car_age = current_year - self.model_year
        self.current_value = round(self.purchase_price * (1 - depreciation_rate) ** car_age)
    
    # TODO: Define print_info() method to output model_year, purchase_price, and current_value


if __name__ == "__main__":    
    year = int(input()) 
    price = int(input())
    current_year = int(input())
    
    my_car = Car()
    my_car.model_year = year
    my_car.purchase_price = price
    my_car.calc_current_value(current_year)
    my_car.print_info()

Water

  Protein: 0.00 g

M&M's
10.0
34.0
2.0
3.0

Nutritional information per serving of M&M's:
  Fat: 10.00 g
  Carbohydrates: 34.00 g
  Protein: 2.00 g

Number of calories for 3.00 serving(s): 702.00

    # TODO: Define constructor with parameters to initialize instance

        return calories

        print(f'Nutritional information per serving of {self.name}:')
        print(f'  Fat: {self.fat:.2f} g')
        print(f'  Carbohydrates: {self.carbs:.2f} g')
        print(f'  Protein: {self.protein:.2f} g')

    item_name = input()

    else:
        amount_fat = float(input())
        amount_carbs = float(input())

        print(f'Number of calories for {num_servings:.2f} serving(s): {food_item.get_calories(num_servings):.2f}')

    def __init__(self):
        self.base = 0
        self.height = 0

        self.base = user_base

        print(f'Height: {self.height:.2f}')

        self.losses = 0

    # TODO: Define get_win_percentage()

    team.print_standing()

9.16 LAB: Vending machine

Given two integers as user inputs that represent the number of drinks to buy and the number of bottles to restock, create a VendingMachine object that performs the following operations:

  • Purchases input number of drinks
  • Restocks input number of bottles
  • Reports inventory

A VendingMachine's initial inventory is 20 drinks.

Ex: If the input is:

5
2

the output is:

Inventory: 17 bottles

# Starter Code :

class VendingMachine:
    def __init__(self):
        self.bottles = 20
        
    def purchase(self, amount):
        self.bottles = self.bottles - amount
      
    def restock(self, amount):
        self.bottles = self.bottles + amount
    
    def get_inventory(self):
        return self.bottles
        
    def report(self):
        print(f'Inventory: {self.bottles} bottles')

Assignment: The Birthday Problem – How Many People for a 50% Chance?

Big Question

We want to answer this:

How many people do we need in a room so that there is about a 50% chance that at least two people share the same birthday (same month and day)?

We already know:

  • With 1 person, there is no chance of a match (you need at least two people to compare).

  • With 367 people, there is 100% certainty, because there are more people than possible birthdays (366 if you include Feb 29, 365 if you don’t).

Somewhere between those two numbers is the smallest number of people that gives us about a 50% chance of a shared birthday.

Your job is to find and justify that number.

Assumptions

Unless you clearly say otherwise, use these assumptions:

  • There are 365 days in a year (ignore leap years).

  • All birthdays are equally likely.

  • People’s birthdays are independent of each other.

If you change any of these assumptions, you must explain what you changed and why.

How You Can Solve It

You can choose one of these main approaches (or do both, if you’re feeling fancy):

Option 1: Mathematical / Formula Approach

  • Find the equations that give the probability of:

    • No shared birthdays among n people, and

    • At least one shared birthday among n people.

  • Use those equations to find the smallest n where the probability of a match is about 50%.

  • Show your work and explain your steps in words that a classmate could understand.

Option 2: Monte Carlo Simulation (Programming)

  • Write a program that:

    • Simulates a room with n randomly generated birthdays.

    • Checks whether there is a birthday match.

    • Repeats this many times (hundreds or thousands of trials).

  • Gradually adjust n and estimate the probability of a match for each n.

  • Use your results to find the smallest n that gives about a 50% match rate.

Required Pieces (Deliverables)

You will turn in:

  1. Written Explanation (Short Report)

    • State the question in your own words.

    • Explain which approach you chose (math, simulation, or both).

    • Clearly state your final answer:

      “We need about ___ people in the room to have a 50% chance of a shared birthday.”

    • Briefly explain why you trust your answer.

  2. Code (if you do a simulation)

    • Submit your code (Python, etc.).

    • Your code should be readable and commented so that another student could follow it.

  3. Learning Journal (Documentation)

    • This is very important.

    • For each search or AI/chat query you do (Google, ChatGPT, etc.), write down:

      • What you searched/asked.

      • What you found.

      • How you feel about it (Helpful? Confusing? Do you trust it? Why or why not?).

    • The goal is to help you notice how you are learning, not just the final answer.

  4. Code Review

    • Use either:

      • An automated tool (like a linter, style checker, etc.), or

      • A human review (a friend/classmate reads your code and gives feedback).

    • In your write-up, briefly summarize:

      • What the review tool/person said.

      • What you changed (if anything) because of the review.

  5. Code Quiz (About Your Own Code)

    • Write 3–5 short questions about your own code (like a mini quiz).

    • Then answer your own questions.

    • Example questions:

      • “What does this loop do?”

      • “Why did I choose this data structure?”

      • “What does this function return and when?”

Optional Bonus Opportunities

These are extra credit, not required.

  • 🎨 Seaborn Visualizations

    • Use Seaborn (a Python plotting library) to make at least one good visualization of your results.

    • For extra-extra bonus, explain in your journal or write-up:

      • Why Seaborn is helpful compared to just using plain matplotlib (for example: nicer defaults, easier styling, better statistical plots).

  • 🎲 Multiple Rooms / Repeated Experiments

    • Run your simulation for the same number of people many times and talk about:

      • How much your estimated probability varies.

      • How confident you feel in your answer.

    • Use language like: “When we ran 1,000 trials, the probability stayed between __ and __ most of the time.”

Grading Rubric (Suggested 100-Point Scale)

You can paste this into Canvas as a rubric.

1. Understanding the Problem (10 points)

  • 9–10: Clearly explains the birthday problem in their own words and correctly describes what “50% chance of a match” means.

  • 6–8: Basic description is correct but missing some clarity or detail.

  • 3–5: Shows partial understanding; some confusion about what is being calculated.

  • 0–2: Major misunderstandings; does not clearly describe the goal.

2. Mathematical / Simulation Approach (Correctness) (25 points)

(Pick the row that fits the student’s chosen method; if they do both, grade the stronger one and optionally award extra credit elsewhere.)

  • 21–25:

    • Math: Correct formulas, correct logic, and correct approximate answer.

    • Simulation: Code correctly simulates the problem, uses enough trials, and arrives at a reasonable estimate near the true answer.

  • 16–20: Mostly correct, with small mistakes that don’t seriously damage the conclusion.

  • 11–15: Some correct ideas, but noticeable errors in formulas, logic, or simulation setup.

  • 0–10: Serious mistakes; approach does not meaningfully answer the question.

3. Learning Journal / Documentation (20 points)

  • 18–20: Journal is detailed and honest. For most searches/queries, includes:

    • What they searched or asked.

    • What they found.

    • How they felt about it (trust, confusion, usefulness).

  • 14–17: Several entries with good detail, but a few are thin or missing reflection.

  • 8–13: Journal exists but is brief, inconsistent, or missing important parts.

  • 0–7: Little to no journal, or only one or two minimal entries.

4. Code Quality & Code Review (15 points)

  • 13–15:

    • Code is readable and reasonably well-organized.

    • Variable names are meaningful.

    • Comments help explain non-obvious parts.

    • A code review (tool or human) is done and summarized clearly, including any changes made.

  • 9–12:

    • Code mostly works and is somewhat readable.

    • Some comments and decent structure.

    • Code review is mentioned but not deeply discussed.

  • 4–8:

    • Code is hard to read or poorly structured.

    • Few or no comments.

    • Little or no evidence of a code review.

  • 0–3:

    • Code missing, non-functional, or unreadable; no code review.

5. Code Quiz (About Their Own Code) (10 points)

  • 9–10:

    • Includes 3–5 thoughtful questions about their own code.

    • Answers show real understanding of what the code is doing and why.

  • 6–8:

    • Questions and answers are present but somewhat shallow.

  • 3–5:

    • Very basic questions; answers don’t show much understanding.

  • 0–2:

    • Missing or nearly missing.

6. Analysis & Interpretation of Results (15 points)

  • 13–15:

    • Clearly states their final answer (approximate number of people).

    • Connects the answer back to the method (math or simulation).

    • Shows some reflection on whether the answer makes sense and how confident they are.

  • 9–12:

    • Answer is stated, but explanation is brief or a bit unclear.

  • 4–8:

    • Answer may be present but not clearly justified.

  • 0–3:

    • No clear final answer or justification.

7. Extra Credit / Bonus (up to +10 points)

These points are added on top of the base 100, at your discretion.

  • Seaborn Visualization Used Well: +0 to 3

    • At least one meaningful Seaborn plot that helps interpret the results.

  • Explains Why Seaborn Is Useful: +0 to 3

    • Student clearly explains why Seaborn is helpful (e.g., nicer defaults, easier complex plots, good integration with DataFrames).

  • Multiple Rooms / Confidence Discussion: +0 to 4

    • Student runs multiple sets of trials and talks about variability and confidence in their results.

# Coding Odyssey 2

[redacted-external-doc-link]

The Google doc is our goals for this week.

**Instructor: Jeremy Evert**  
**Contact: Email - [redacted-instructor-email] | Text - [redacted-instructor-phone]**  

## Objective:
This assignment aims to encourage you to apply the programming concepts and tools you have learned in class to build a project of your choice. The goal is to foster creativity, problem-solving, and practical application of theoretical knowledge.

## Assignment Guidelines:

1. **Project Selection**:
   - Choose a project idea that interests you. It can be a game, a utility, a simulation, or any other application.
   - Ensure that your project incorporates most of the concepts we have covered in class, including but not limited to:
     - Variables and Data Types
     - Control Structures (loops, conditionals)
     - Functions and Modular Programming
     - Basic Data Structures (lists, dictionaries)
     - File I/O
     - Error Handling
     - (Optional) Basic GUI elements (if you wish to explore)

2. **Design Phase**:
   - **Design Document**: Create a design document outlining the following:
     - **Project Title**: Name of your project.
     - **Description**: A brief overview of what your project does.
     - **Features**: List the main features of your project.
     - **Tools/Technologies**: Identify the tools, libraries, and languages you will use.
     - **Flowchart/Diagram**: Provide a flowchart or diagram of your program’s architecture.
     - **Milestones**: Break down your project into smaller tasks or milestones.

3. **Implementation Phase**:
   - Start coding your project based on your design document.
   - Ensure that you write clean, readable, and well-documented code.
   - Use version control (e.g., Git) to track your progress and changes.

4. **Testing and Debugging**:
   - Test your code regularly to catch and fix bugs early.
   - Ensure that your code handles errors gracefully and includes appropriate error messages.

5. **Final Submission**:
   - Submit the following:
     - **Design Document**: Updated if there were any changes during implementation.
     - **Source Code**: All the code files of your project.
     - **Readme File**: Instructions on how to run your project, any dependencies, and a brief user guide.
     - **Demonstration**: (Optional) A short video or presentation demonstrating your project.

## Grading Structure:

- **Base Points (Not Stacking)**:
  - **25 Points**: You have a design for your idea.
  - **50 Points**: You have a design and some code.
  - **75 Points**: You have a design and some of your code runs.
  - **100 Points**: You have a design and a working code.

- **Bonus Points**:
  - **Creativity**: Innovative and original ideas.
  - **Efficiency**: Optimal use of resources and efficient algorithms.
  - **Enjoyment**: Fun and engaging user experience.
  - **Clean Code**: Well-structured, commented, and readable code.

## Submission:
- Submit your project through the course’s submission portal or email it directly to [redacted-instructor-email] by the due date.

## Tips for Success:
- **Plan Ahead**: Start with a clear plan and follow it.
- **Stay Organized**: Keep your code and resources well-organized.
- **Seek Help**: If you encounter any issues, feel free to reach out for help.
- **Experiment and Learn**: Don’t be afraid to try new things and learn from them.

Good luck, and happy coding!

---

This version provides a clear structure and detailed requirements, helping students understand the expectations and steps involved in completing the assignment.

  - **Efficiency**: Optimal use of resources and efficient algorithms.

## Submission:

# Coding Odyssey 3

**Instructor: Jeremy Evert**  
**Contact: Email - [redacted-instructor-email] | Text - [redacted-instructor-phone]**  

## Objective:
This assignment aims to encourage you to apply the programming concepts and tools you have learned in class to build a project of your choice. The goal is to foster creativity, problem-solving, and practical application of theoretical knowledge.

## Assignment Guidelines:

1. **Project Selection**:
   - Choose a project idea that interests you. It can be a game, a utility, a simulation, or any other application.
   - Ensure that your project incorporates most of the concepts we have covered in class, including but not limited to:
     - Variables and Data Types
     - Control Structures (loops, conditionals)
     - Functions and Modular Programming
     - Basic Data Structures (lists, dictionaries)
     - File I/O
     - Error Handling
     - (Optional) Basic GUI elements (if you wish to explore)

2. **Design Phase**:
   - **Design Document**: Create a design document outlining the following:
     - **Project Title**: Name of your project.
     - **Description**: A brief overview of what your project does.
     - **Features**: List the main features of your project.
     - **Tools/Technologies**: Identify the tools, libraries, and languages you will use.
     - **Flowchart/Diagram**: Provide a flowchart or diagram of your program’s architecture.
     - **Milestones**: Break down your project into smaller tasks or milestones.

3. **Implementation Phase**:
   - Start coding your project based on your design document.
   - Ensure that you write clean, readable, and well-documented code.
   - Use version control (e.g., Git) to track your progress and changes.

4. **Testing and Debugging**:
   - Test your code regularly to catch and fix bugs early.
   - Ensure that your code handles errors gracefully and includes appropriate error messages.

5. **Final Submission**:
   - Submit the following:
     - **Design Document**: Updated if there were any changes during implementation.
     - **Source Code**: All the code files of your project.
     - **Readme File**: Instructions on how to run your project, any dependencies, and a brief user guide.
     - **Demonstration**: (Optional) A short video or presentation demonstrating your project.

## Grading Structure:

- **Base Points (Not Stacking)**:
  - **25 Points**: You have a design for your idea.
  - **50 Points**: You have a design and some code.
  - **75 Points**: You have a design and some of your code runs.
  - **100 Points**: You have a design and a working code.

- **Bonus Points**:
  - **Creativity**: Innovative and original ideas.
  - **Efficiency**: Optimal use of resources and efficient algorithms.
  - **Enjoyment**: Fun and engaging user experience.
  - **Clean Code**: Well-structured, commented, and readable code.

## Submission:
- Submit your project through the course’s submission portal or email it directly to [redacted-instructor-email] by the due date.

## Tips for Success:
- **Plan Ahead**: Start with a clear plan and follow it.
- **Stay Organized**: Keep your code and resources well-organized.
- **Seek Help**: If you encounter any issues, feel free to reach out for help.
- **Experiment and Learn**: Don’t be afraid to try new things and learn from them.

Good luck, and happy coding!

This is a bonus assignment for the face to face class who will do a group activity in class.


The online students are welcome to complete some of the LinkedIn learning modules on git and GitHub 



Exercise: Collaborative Document Editing

  1. Create a Repository

    • Student A creates a new repository on GitHub and initializes it with a README file.

  2. Invite Collaborator

    • Student A invites Student B to the repository as a collaborator.

  3. Create a New Branch

    • Both students create their own branches from the main branch. Let’s say Student A creates a branch named student-a-edits and Student B creates student-b-edits.

  4. Make Changes

    • Each student makes some changes to the README file in their respective branches. They can add some text or modify the existing content.

  5. Commit and Push Changes

    • After making the changes, each student commits the changes with a suitable commit message and pushes the changes to their respective branches on GitHub.

  6. Create Pull Requests

    • Both students create a pull request to merge their branches into the main branch. In the pull request description, they can describe the changes they made.

  7. Review Pull Requests

    • Each student reviews the other’s pull request, adds comments if necessary, and if everything looks good, they approve the pull request.

  8. Merge Pull Requests

    • After approval, each student merges the other’s pull request. If there are any merge conflicts, they will need to resolve them before the merge can be completed.

  9. Pull Changes

    • Finally, both students pull the changes from the main branch to their local repositories to get the latest version of the README file.

 

 

And here is a more fun version:

Exercise: The Great Cookie Caper

  1. Create a Repository

    • Student A creates a new repository on GitHub named “CookieCaper” and initializes it with a README file.

  2. Invite Collaborator

    • Student A invites Student B to the repository as a collaborator.

  3. Create a New Branch

    • Both students create their own branches from the main branch. Let’s say Student A creates a branch named cookie-design and Student B creates bank-plan.

  4. Make Changes

    • Student A adds a recipe for the special cookie in the cookie-design branch.
    • Student B outlines a silly plan for the bank heist in the bank-plan branch.

  5. Commit and Push Changes

    • After making the changes, each student commits the changes with a suitable commit message and pushes the changes to their respective branches on GitHub.

  6. Create Pull Requests

    • Both students create a pull request to merge their branches into the main branch. They review each other’s work and suggest changes.

  7. Merge Pull Requests

    • After reviewing and approving the changes, they merge the pull requests. Now, the main branch has both the cookie recipe and the bank heist plan.

And here’s a cheat sheet for Git:

Git Cheat Sheet

  • git init: Initialize a new Git repository.
  • git clone [url]: Clone a repository that exists on GitHub.
  • git branch [branch-name]: Create a new branch.
  • git checkout [branch-name]: Switch to a specific branch.
  • git add [file-name]: Add a file to the staging area.
  • git commit -m “[commit message]”: Commit changes with a message.
  • git push origin [branch-name]: Push changes to a remote repository.
  • git pull origin [branch-name]: Update local repository to the newest commit.
  • git merge [branch-name]: Merge a branch into the active branch.

Remember, Git is a powerful tool for team collaboration. It allows multiple people to work on a project without overwriting each other’s changes. Happy coding!

  • Communication: Regularly discuss your thought process with your partner. Clear communication will help you both understand the problem better and develop a shared solution.
  • Weekly Role Assignment: Each week, one partner will take on the role of the “driver” (the person typing the code), while the other will be the “navigator” (the person reviewing and suggesting improvements). Only the driver should be actively working on the code during that week’s assignment.
  • Partners should alternate roles each week so that both of you gain experience in both driving and mentoring.
  • Respect and Patience: Listen to your partner’s ideas, and be open to different approaches. Be patient, especially if your partner is struggling with a concept.
  • Reflection: After completing the assignment, take a few minutes to discuss what you learned, what challenges you faced, and how you overcame them.

  • Ask Detailed Questions: Don’t just ask for the solution. Instead, ask ChatGPT to explain concepts, provide examples, or suggest alternative approaches.
  • Understand the Code: Before moving forward, make sure you understand every line of code provided by ChatGPT. Ask follow-up questions if something is unclear.
  • Experiment: Use ChatGPT to explore different ways of solving the problem. Try out variations of the code and ask about the pros and cons of each approach.
  • Learn by Teaching: Explain your understanding to ChatGPT. Teaching back to the AI can reinforce your learning and highlight any gaps in your knowledge.

    • Optional: Instead of a brief text entry, you can upload a video summarizing your collaboration and discussing your roles.

Grading: This assignment is graded on a pass-fail basis. However, those who submit a complete in-class pair programming assignment will receive double points as a bonus. Your submission should demonstrate a clear understanding of the problem and a thoughtful approach to learning.

assignments.description:
Progress Report Assignment: Progress Report.docx

Progress Report Assignment

Welcome to your next assignment! We are going to work on something called a Progress Report. This report is provided by the registrar's office and tells you exactly what you need to graduate. It contains similar information to a degree sheet but is customized to show what you already have credit for and what you are missing. The report is broken down by area for easier understanding.

Assignment Instructions

  1. Obtain Your Progress Report:
    • Log in to self service, which is one of the options on single sign-on where you access Canvas and email.
    • Once inside self-service, search for Progress Report.
    • Download a digital copy of your report. Please export this as a PDF and upload it for your assignment.
  1. Review the Report:
    • Examine each area listed in your progress report.
    • Identify the courses you have completed and the credits you have earned.
    • Note any areas where you are missing credits or required courses.
  1. Document Missing Requirements:
    • Create a list of courses and credits you still need to complete your degree.
    • Include details such as the course name, number of credits, and the specific requirement it fulfills.
  1. Set Academic Goals:
    • Based on your review, set realistic academic goals for the upcoming semesters.
    • Plan out which courses you need to take and when you will take them.
  1. Prepare a Report:
    • Write a summary of your findings, including the courses you have completed and the ones you still need to take.
    • Outline your academic plan and goals for completing your degree.
  1. Submit Your Assignment:
    • Upload your progress report and your written summary to the assignment submission section.
    • Ensure all documents are clearly labeled with your name and student ID.

If you have any questions or need further assistance, don't hesitate to reach out to me. Let's make sure you're on the right track to achieving your academic goals!

 

Please make a comment if you have any questions about what is required for you to graduate. 

Please email me at [redacted-instructor-email] if there is anything unexpected. Or you can text me at [redacted-instructor-phone].

Unofficial Transcript Assignment: Unofficial Transcript.docx

 

Hey everyone! Welcome to the start of the semester. I'm thrilled to embark on this academic adventure with you. Remember, you have the power to take charge of your own success. Don't hesitate to reach out to me if you need any help along the way. By taking ownership of your studies, you'll gain confidence, perform better academically, and set yourself up for success after graduation. Let's make this semester great together!

 

As we start this journey, it's important to review your academic progress towards graduation. Your official university academic record is called your transcript. For this exercise, we'll begin with your unofficial transcript. Remember, this assignment is not just about earning points. It's a chance to take a close look at your academic progress, think about the classes you want to take, and set goals for your GPA. By examining your unofficial transcript, you'll get a clearer picture of where you stand and what you can do to achieve your academic goals. Here's a step-by-step guide to help you through the process:

Step-by-Step Guide to Reviewing Your Unofficial Transcript

  1. Obtain Your Unofficial Transcript:
    • Log in to your student portal.
    • Navigate to the section where you can view or download your unofficial transcript.
    • Download a digital copy of your transcript. This is what is graded for your assignment.
  1. Check Course Enrollment:
    • Compare the courses you are currently enrolled in with your transcript.
    • Ensure you are not enrolled in any courses for which you have already received credit.
    • Note any discrepancies, such as being enrolled in a course you have previously completed successfully.
  1. Verify Grades:
    • Review the grades listed for each course.
    • Confirm that the grades match your expectations based on your performance.
    • Highlight any grades that are not what you expected or are missing.
    • Reach out to the instructor for any class with a problem. Ask them what their grade change policy is.

 


  • Review Tuition and Credits:
  • Check that all courses you have paid tuition for are listed on the transcript.
  • Ensure that all credits you have earned are accurately reflected.
  • Verify that there are no missing courses or discrepancies in credit hours.
  • Identify Unexpected Items:
  • Look for any courses, grades, or credits that are unexpected.
  • Make a note of any anomalies or surprises that need further investigation.
  • Reach out to your advisor or academic records in the Registrar’s office and find out what you can about anything that does not make sense to you.
  • Document Your Findings:
  • Create a list of any issues or unexpected findings from your review.
  • Include details such as the course name, expected vs. actual grade, and any discrepancies in enrollment or credits.
  • Contact Your Instructor:
  • Prepare an email or text message to your instructor with your findings.
  • Be clear and concise, providing specific details about the discrepancies.

Email Template

Here’s a sample email template you can use to report any discrepancies to your instructor:

 


Subject: Discrepancies Found in Unofficial Transcript

Dear Professor Evert,

I have reviewed my unofficial transcript closely and have identified a few discrepancies that I need your assistance with:

  1. Duplicate Course Enrollment:
    • Course: [Course Name]
    • Issue: I am currently enrolled in this course but have already received credit for it previously.
  1. Unexpected Grades:
    • Course: [Course Name]
    • Expected Grade: [Expected Grade]
    • Actual Grade: [Actual Grade]
  1. Missing Course/Credit:
    • Course: [Course Name]
    • Issue: This course, for which I have paid tuition, is missing from my transcript.

I have attached a copy of my unofficial transcript for your reference. Please let me know how we can resolve these issues.

Thank you for your assistance.

Best regards, [Your Name] [Your Student ID]

 

 

Text Message Template

 

If you prefer to send a text message, here’s a shorter version:

 


Hi Prof. Evert, this is [Your Name, Student ID]. I've found a few discrepancies in my unofficial transcript:

  1. Duplicate course enrollment in [Course Name].
  2. Unexpected grade in [Course Name] (Expected: [Grade], Actual: [Grade]).
  3. Missing course/credit for [Course Name]. Please advise on how to resolve these. Thanks!


Final Steps

  • Send Your Communication: Your teacher for this class cannot change your grade for a previous class. Email or text your previous instructor with the documented discrepancies.
  • Follow Up: If you do not receive a response within a few days, follow up with another email or text to ensure your concerns are addressed.

By carefully reviewing your unofficial transcript and promptly addressing any issues with your instructor, you can ensure that your academic record is accurate and complete.

### Resume Assignment

For this assignment, you will create or update your resume to reflect your current work experience, education, and accomplishments. Your resume will be a living document that you will continue to build on throughout the semester. Follow the instructions below to complete the assignment and make your resume stand out.

### Assignment Instructions

1. **Create or Update Your Resume:**
   - Include sections for contact information, work experience, education, skills, and accomplishments.
   - If you are a recent high school graduate, include relevant high school achievements. If you have been out of school for a while, focus on more recent accomplishments.

2. **Save and Maintain Your Resume:**
   - Save your resume as a digital document. You will be adding to it and refining it throughout the semester.

3. **Seek Feedback:**
   - Visit Career Services or the Writing Center for assistance with your resume.
   - Ask your advisor, teachers, and mentors from your community to review your resume and provide feedback.
   - Consider watching LinkedIn Learning videos on resume writing for additional tips.

4. **Use the 3-2-1 Plan for Continuous Improvement:**
   - **Daily:** Set an alarm to spend five minutes writing down three things you accomplished that day.
   - **Weekly:** Set a calendar reminder to spend 30 minutes adding two things you achieved that week to your Curriculum Vitae (CV).
   - **Monthly:** Set a monthly calendar reminder to dedicate an hour to updating your resume, adding at least one new bullet point each month.

### Tips and Tricks for a Great Resume

- **Tailor Your Resume:** Customize your resume for each job application by highlighting the most relevant experience and skills.
- **Use Action Verbs:** Start each bullet point with a strong action verb (e.g., "developed," "managed," "led") to convey your achievements effectively.
- **Quantify Achievements:** Whenever possible, use numbers to quantify your accomplishments (e.g., "Increased sales by 20%" or "Managed a team of 10").
- **Keep It Concise:** Aim for a one-page resume if you have less than 10 years of experience. Ensure it is easy to read with clear headings and bullet points.
- **Professional Appearance:** Use a clean, professional format with consistent fonts and spacing. Avoid using overly decorative elements that may distract from the content.

### Submission

- Save your resume as a PDF.
- Upload the PDF to the assignment submission section.

Dream Job Reflection Paper

Purpose

This assignment helps you define your real dream job and connect it to your current skills, education, and goals. You’ll research a real career, analyze how it fits you, and reflect on how achieving it could shape your life.

Think of it as designing your future career path—not just imagining it.

Step 1: Choose Your Dream Job

Pick a real job title from a credible listing (Indeed, USAJobs, company site, etc.). Include the link or reference.

Your job should be:

  • A position you could realistically qualify for within 5–10 years.

  • Something that excites you—not just something that pays well.

Step 2: Research the Job

Find details about:

  • Education & Certifications required

  • Skills & Tools used

  • Typical Work Environment

  • Career Growth Opportunities

Use at least 2 credible sources (like the Bureau of Labor Statistics, company websites, or professional organizations). Include citations.

Step 3: Write Your Essay

Length: 2–3 pages, double-spaced
Format: 12-point Times New Roman, 1-inch margins

Organize your paper with the following sections:

a) Why This Is Your Dream Job

  • What draws you to it?

  • What inspired your interest?

  • What impact do you want to make?

b) How It Fits You

  • What skills or experiences make you a good fit?

  • How does it align with your interests and personality?

  • What new skills will you need to develop?

c) How It Would Impact Your Life

  • How would this job affect your happiness, stability, or growth?

  • What personal values or goals does it support?

  • What challenges might come with it?

(Optional) d) Your 5-Year Plan

  • What steps will you take to get there—courses, degrees, certifications, or internships?

Step 4: Proof and Submit

  • Read your essay aloud before submitting.

  • Save as a PDF and upload to Canvas.

Ask yourself:

  • Does my essay sound like me?

  • Would someone understand why this job matters to me?

  • Did I include both research and personal reflection?

Grading Rubric (10 Points Total)

Category Excellent (9–10) Proficient (7–8) Developing (5–6) Needs Work (0–4)
Career Research Multiple credible sources; deep understanding of the profession. Some research; basic overview provided. Minimal detail; unclear job info. No research included.
Personal Connection Strong, authentic connection; clear passion. Some personal connection shown. Weak or generic link to self. No personal tie explained.
Analysis & Reflection Insightful; connects growth, skills, and goals. Some reflection; missing depth. Limited or surface-level analysis. No reflection; mostly summary.
Organization & Writing Logical flow; clear, professional tone; minimal errors. Generally organized; few grammar issues. Some disorganization or grammar errors. Disorganized; many errors.
Formatting & Citations Meets all format rules; cites sources properly. Minor formatting issues. Missing a few required elements. Formatting incomplete or missing citations.

Questions?
Email [redacted-instructor-email] or text [redacted-instructor-phone] for help.

Professional Skillset Gap Analysis — 10 Points

Purpose

This short reflection helps you think like a professional:

  • What job do you want?

  • What skills do you already have?

  • What skills do you still need?

  • What’s your plan to close that gap?

Instructions

1. Name Your Goal Job

  • Pick a specific role that excites you (for example, Network Engineer, Forensic Chemist, Mechanical Designer).

  • Look up the top skills or certifications employers ask for in that job.

2. Rate Your Current Skills
Make a simple list or table. Use a 1–5 scale where 5 = job ready.

Skill Current (1–5) Needed (1–5) Gap
Example: CAD Software 3 5 2

Include both technical (hard) skills and interpersonal (soft) skills.

3. Make an Action Plan

  • For each major gap, list a few clear steps you can take this year.
    Examples: take a course, earn a certificate, ask to shadow a professional, join a club, build a project, or find an internship.

  • Add when you plan to complete each step (this semester, within a year, before graduation, etc.).

4. Write a Short Reflection (1–2 paragraphs)
Explain what you learned about yourself.

  • What are your top strengths right now?

  • Which gaps will make the biggest difference when you close them?

  • How will your plan help you grow into your dream job?

Submission

  • 1–2 pages total.

  • Include: your goal job, skill chart, action plan, and reflection.

  • Save and upload as a PDF to Canvas.

Pro Tips

  • Be honest and specific — this isn’t about perfection, it’s about direction.

  • Add numbers to visualize your progress (the “Gavin Crawford method”).

  • Focus on actions, not just wishes — clear steps make the plan real.

  • Strong submissions usually sound like this: “Right now I’m at a 3 in public speaking. I’ll raise it to a 4 by presenting twice this semester in class and joining a student club.”

Why It Matters

This isn’t just a class task — it’s your personal roadmap. The more clearly you identify your gaps and next steps now, the faster you’ll grow into the professional you want to become.

### Professional Networking Assignment

#### Purpose

This assignment is designed to help you develop and maintain professional relationships in your desired field. Networking is a crucial skill that can open doors to job opportunities, provide valuable industry insights, and help you build a support system of like-minded professionals.

#### Instructions

1. **Research Professional Events and Organizations:**
   - Identify professional events, such as conferences, meetups, webinars, and workshops, related to your dream job.
   - Look for professional organizations and societies in your field. For example, if you are in Computer Science, consider groups like ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) or IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers).

2. **Attend at Least One Event:**
   - Choose an event that fits your schedule and aligns with your career interests.
   - Participate actively in the event, whether it is virtual or in-person.
   - Make an effort to connect with 2-3 professionals in your field. Prepare a brief introduction about yourself and have some questions ready to ask.

3. **Follow Up with Contacts:**
   - After the event, follow up with the contacts you made.
   - Send a personalized email or LinkedIn message thanking them for their time and referencing your conversation.
   - If appropriate, suggest a follow-up meeting or ask if you can stay in touch for future advice and opportunities.

4. **Reflect on Your Experience:**
   - Write a reflection on your networking experience.
   - Discuss the insights you gained from the event and the connections you made.
   - Reflect on how this experience has impacted your understanding of the industry and your career goals.

#### Tips for Technical Career Fields

- **Computer Science & Software Engineering:**
  - Attend hackathons, coding bootcamps, and tech meetups.
  - Join online forums and communities like Stack Overflow, GitHub, and Reddit.
  - Participate in open-source projects to showcase your skills and collaborate with others.

- **Engineering Technology:**
  - Attend industry trade shows, technology expos, and engineering summits.
  - Join organizations like the National Society of Professional Engineers (NSPE) or the Society of Manufacturing Engineers (SME).
  - Engage in local chapter events and online webinars.

- **Physics:**
  - Attend physics conferences, seminars, and symposiums.
  - Join professional societies like the American Physical Society (APS) or the Institute of Physics (IOP).

# Coding Odyssey 1

**Instructor: Jeremy Evert**  
**Contact: Email - [redacted-instructor-email] | Text - [redacted-instructor-phone]**  

## Objective:
This assignment aims to encourage you to apply the programming concepts and tools you have learned in class to build a project of your choice. The goal is to foster creativity, problem-solving, and practical application of theoretical knowledge.

## Assignment Guidelines:

1. **Project Selection**:
   - Choose a project idea that interests you. It can be a game, a utility, a simulation, or any other application.
   - Ensure that your project incorporates most of the concepts we have covered in class, including but not limited to:
     - Variables and Data Types
     - Control Structures (loops, conditionals)
     - Functions and Modular Programming
     - Basic Data Structures (lists, dictionaries)
     - File I/O
     - Error Handling
     - (Optional) Basic GUI elements (if you wish to explore)

2. **Design Phase**:
   - **Design Document**: Create a design document outlining the following:
     - **Project Title**: Name of your project.
     - **Description**: A brief overview of what your project does.
     - **Features**: List the main features of your project.
     - **Tools/Technologies**: Identify the tools, libraries, and languages you will use.
     - **Flowchart/Diagram**: Provide a flowchart or diagram of your program’s architecture.
     - **Milestones**: Break down your project into smaller tasks or milestones.

3. **Implementation Phase**:
   - Start coding your project based on your design document.
   - Ensure that you write clean, readable, and well-documented code.
   - Use version control (e.g., Git) to track your progress and changes.

4. **Testing and Debugging**:
   - Test your code regularly to catch and fix bugs early.
   - Ensure that your code handles errors gracefully and includes appropriate error messages.

discussion_topics.title: The Monty Hall Problem
discussion_topics.message:
In the Monty Hall problem, you’re on a game show with 3 doors:

  • Behind 1 door: a car (win!) 🚗

  • Behind the other 2 doors: goats 🐐🐐

You pick a door.
The host (who knows where the car is) then opens one of the other two doors, always showing a goat.

Now you’re given a choice:

  • Stay with your original door

  • Switch to the other unopened door

What should you do?

assignment.description: How many people need to be in a room before it’s more likely than not (over 50%) that at least two share the same birthday?
assignment.name: The Birthday Problem

discussion_topics.title: End of Semester Project
discussion_topics.message:
Assignment: The Birthday Problem – How Many People for a 50% Chance?

Big Question

We want to answer this:

How many people do we need in a room so that there is about a 50% chance that at least two people share the same birthday (same month and day)?

We already know:

  • With 1 person, there is no chance of a match (you need at least two people to compare).

  • With 367 people, there is 100% certainty, because there are more people than possible birthdays (366 if you include Feb 29, 365 if you don’t).

Somewhere between those two numbers is the smallest number of people that gives us about a 50% chance of a shared birthday.

Your job is to find and justify that number.

Assumptions

Unless you clearly say otherwise, use these assumptions:

  • There are 365 days in a year (ignore leap years).

  • All birthdays are equally likely.

  • People’s birthdays are independent of each other.

If you change any of these assumptions, you must explain what you changed and why.

How You Can Solve It

You can choose one of these main approaches (or do both, if you’re feeling fancy):

Option 1: Mathematical / Formula Approach

  • Find the equations that give the probability of:

    • No shared birthdays among n people, and

    • At least one shared birthday among n people.

  • Use those equations to find the smallest n where the probability of a match is about 50%.

  • Show your work and explain your steps in words that a classmate could understand.

Option 2: Monte Carlo Simulation (Programming)

  • Write a program that:

    • Simulates a room with n randomly generated birthdays.

    • Checks whether there is a birthday match.

    • Repeats this many times (hundreds or thousands of trials).

  • Gradually adjust n and estimate the probability of a match for each n.

  • Use your results to find the smallest n that gives about a 50% match rate.

Required Pieces (Deliverables)

You will turn in:

  1. Written Explanation (Short Report)

    • State the question in your own words.

    • Explain which approach you chose (math, simulation, or both).

    • Clearly state your final answer:

      “We need about ___ people in the room to have a 50% chance of a shared birthday.”

    • Briefly explain why you trust your answer.

  2. Code (if you do a simulation)

    • Submit your code (Python, etc.).

    • Your code should be readable and commented so that another student could follow it.

  3. Learning Journal (Documentation)

    • This is very important.

    • For each search or AI/chat query you do (Google, ChatGPT, etc.), write down:

      • What you searched/asked.

      • What you found.

      • How you feel about it (Helpful? Confusing? Do you trust it? Why or why not?).

    • The goal is to help you notice how you are learning, not just the final answer.

  4. Code Review

    • Use either:

      • An automated tool (like a linter, style checker, etc.), or

      • A human review (a friend/classmate reads your code and gives feedback).

    • In your write-up, briefly summarize:

      • What the review tool/person said.

      • What you changed (if anything) because of the review.

  5. Code Quiz (About Your Own Code)

    • Write 3–5 short questions about your own code (like a mini quiz).

    • Then answer your own questions.

    • Example questions:

      • “What does this loop do?”

      • “Why did I choose this data structure?”

      • “What does this function return and when?”

Optional Bonus Opportunities

These are extra credit, not required.

  • 🎨 Seaborn Visualizations

    • Use Seaborn (a Python plotting library) to make at least one good visualization of your results.

    • For extra-extra bonus, explain in your journal or write-up:

      • Why Seaborn is helpful compared to just using plain matplotlib (for example: nicer defaults, easier styling, better statistical plots).

  • 🎲 Multiple Rooms / Repeated Experiments

    • Run your simulation for the same number of people many times and talk about:

      • How much your estimated probability varies.

      • How confident you feel in your answer.

    • Use language like: “When we ran 1,000 trials, the probability stayed between __ and __ most of the time.”

Grading Rubric (Suggested 100-Point Scale)

You can paste this into Canvas as a rubric.

1. Understanding the Problem (10 points)

  • 9–10: Clearly explains the birthday problem in their own words and correctly describes what “50% chance of a match” means.

  • 6–8: Basic description is correct but missing some clarity or detail.

  • 3–5: Shows partial understanding; some confusion about what is being calculated.

  • 0–2: Major misunderstandings; does not clearly describe the goal.

2. Mathematical / Simulation Approach (Correctness) (25 points)

(Pick the row that fits the student’s chosen method; if they do both, grade the stronger one and optionally award extra credit elsewhere.)

  • 21–25:

    • Math: Correct formulas, correct logic, and correct approximate answer.

    • Simulation: Code correctly simulates the problem, uses enough trials, and arrives at a reasonable estimate near the true answer.

  • 16–20: Mostly correct, with small mistakes that don’t seriously damage the conclusion.

  • 11–15: Some correct ideas, but noticeable errors in formulas, logic, or simulation setup.

  • 0–10: Serious mistakes; approach does not meaningfully answer the question.

3. Learning Journal / Documentation (20 points)

  • 18–20: Journal is detailed and honest. For most searches/queries, includes:

    • What they searched or asked.

    • What they found.

    • How they felt about it (trust, confusion, usefulness).

  • 14–17: Several entries with good detail, but a few are thin or missing reflection.

  • 8–13: Journal exists but is brief, inconsistent, or missing important parts.

  • 0–7: Little to no journal, or only one or two minimal entries.

4. Code Quality & Code Review (15 points)

  • 13–15:

    • Code is readable and reasonably well-organized.

    • Variable names are meaningful.

    • Comments help explain non-obvious parts.

    • A code review (tool or human) is done and summarized clearly, including any changes made.

  • 9–12:

    • Code mostly works and is somewhat readable.

    • Some comments and decent structure.

    • Code review is mentioned but not deeply discussed.

  • 4–8:

    • Code is hard to read or poorly structured.

    • Few or no comments.

    • Little or no evidence of a code review.

  • 0–3:

    • Code missing, non-functional, or unreadable; no code review.

5. Code Quiz (About Their Own Code) (10 points)

  • 9–10:

    • Includes 3–5 thoughtful questions about their own code.

    • Answers show real understanding of what the code is doing and why.

  • 6–8:

    • Questions and answers are present but somewhat shallow.

  • 3–5:

    • Very basic questions; answers don’t show much understanding.

  • 0–2:

    • Missing or nearly missing.

6. Analysis & Interpretation of Results (15 points)

  • 13–15:

    • Clearly states their final answer (approximate number of people).

    • Connects the answer back to the method (math or simulation).

    • Shows some reflection on whether the answer makes sense and how confident they are.

  • 9–12:

    • Answer is stated, but explanation is brief or a bit unclear.

  • 4–8:

    • Answer may be present but not clearly justified.

  • 0–3:

    • No clear final answer or justification.

7. Extra Credit / Bonus (up to +10 points)

These points are added on top of the base 100, at your discretion.

  • Seaborn Visualization Used Well: +0 to 3

    • At least one meaningful Seaborn plot that helps interpret the results.

  • Explains Why Seaborn Is Useful: +0 to 3

    • Student clearly explains why Seaborn is helpful (e.g., nicer defaults, easier complex plots, good integration with DataFrames).

  • Multiple Rooms / Confidence Discussion: +0 to 4

    • Student runs multiple sets of trials and talks about variability and confidence in their results.

Grading Rubric – Birthday Problem Project (100 pts + up to 10 bonus)

Criteria Points Exemplary (Full Credit) Proficient Developing Beginning
1. Problem Understanding & Final Answer 25 pts Clearly restates the birthday problem in their own words and explains what “50% chance of a shared birthday” means. States assumptions (365 days, equal likelihood, etc.) and clearly gives a final answer (“We need about ___ people…”). Explanation is easy for a classmate to follow. Restates the problem mostly correctly and gives a reasonable final answer. Some minor gaps in assumptions or clarity, but the overall idea is right. Shows partial understanding; seems unsure about what probability is being measured or what “50% chance” means. Final answer may be unclear or weakly stated. Major misunderstandings. No clear final answer, or answer is not connected to the problem being asked.
2. Method, Results & Interpretation (Math or Simulation) 25 pts Uses a correct mathematical formula OR simulation. Work is logically organized. For math: formulas and steps are correct and lead to a reasonable 50% estimate. For simulation: code/approach is correctly set up, uses enough trials, and the estimated probability makes sense. Interprets results and comments briefly on how confident they are. Method is mostly correct with minor errors that don’t seriously affect the conclusion. Shows some reasoning and basic interpretation of the results. Some correct ideas, but noticeable errors in formulas, simulation setup, or logic. Interpretation is shallow or confusing; hard to see how the answer was chosen. Method is largely incorrect or missing. Little or no meaningful reasoning or interpretation of results.
3. Code, Code Review & Code Quiz (if student chooses simulation; can be marked N/A for pure-math solutions) 25 pts Code is readable and runs (or very close). Variable names are meaningful; there are comments where needed. Student performs a code review (tool or human) and briefly summarizes what they learned and any changes made. Includes 3–5 self-made questions about their code with answers that show real understanding of what the code does and why. Code mostly works and is somewhat readable. Some comments and decent structure. Code review is mentioned with at least a short summary. Includes a code quiz, but questions/answers are somewhat shallow or mostly factual. Code runs only partially or is hard to read (few comments, messy structure). Code review is very brief or unclear. Code quiz is minimal (e.g., 1–2 simple questions) or shows limited understanding. Code is missing, non-functional, or unreadable. No code review and no meaningful code quiz.
4. Learning Journal & Documentation / Reflection 25 pts Journal is detailed and covers most of the work process. For many searches/AI queries, student records: what they searched, what they found, and how they felt about it (trust, confusion, usefulness). Reflection shows some awareness of how they are learning and improving. Journal has several useful entries with at least some detail on searches and results. Reflection is present but may be brief or inconsistent. Journal exists but is sparse or incomplete. Only a few entries, missing reflection on trust/understanding, or only lists links without commentary. Little to no journal. One or two very short notes, or nothing turned in.

Extra Credit / Bonus (up to +10 pts)

You can add these as separate bonus items in Canvas:

  • Seaborn Visualization (0–3 pts)
    Student uses Seaborn to create at least one meaningful plot that helps interpret probabilities or results.

  • Why Seaborn? (0–3 pts)
    Student briefly explains why Seaborn is useful (e.g., nicer defaults, easier statistical plots, good with DataFrames, clearer visuals).

    Student repeats simulations (or analyzes multiple runs) for the same group size and discusses how the estimated probability varies and how confident they are in their answer.

discussion_topics.message:
Objective: The goal of this assignment is to enhance your programming skills through collaboration with peers or with AI assistance. You will learn to tackle coding challenges effectively, whether by working with a classmate or by utilizing ChatGPT as a learning partner. This assignment emphasizes not just solving the problem but also understanding the process and best practices for learning how to program.

Assignment Overview:

  1. In-Class Pair Programming (Double Points):

discussion_topics.message:
✨ Encouragement & Warm-Up: “Get Your Sheet Together”

Before starting, pairs should pause and write down a few things together. This helps set expectations, clarify goals, and avoid the awkward “so… what are we doing?” moment.

Mentor’s Role: Push the learner to actually complete this before coding begins. The mentor should also take a moment to reflect on their own expectations for the session.

Steps

  1. Set Two Goals (Minimum)

    • Each person states at least two goals.

    • Example goals: “I want to understand loops better,” “I want to practice using Git without fear,” or “I want us to finish a working prototype.”

  2. Define the Project in One Sentence

    • Write a single, simple sentence about the project.

    • Example: “We are making a dice game that calculates scores automatically.”

    • This avoids scope creep and keeps everyone on the same page.

  3. Time Reality Check

    • Each partner says honestly how much time they realistically have between now and the next presentation or deadline.

    • Example: “I’ve got maybe 2 hours this week outside of class,” or “I can do an hour a night until Friday.”

    • Honesty prevents frustration later.

  4. Mentor’s Reflection

    • The mentor writes down 1–2 of their own goals for the session.

    • Example: “I want to guide without taking over the keyboard,” or “I want to give at least 3 meaningful nudges but let them solve the rest.”

Why This Works

  • Alignment: Everyone’s vision is on the same sheet of paper.

  • Accountability: Naming goals makes them more likely to happen.

  • Realism: Knowing actual time commitments keeps expectations grounded.

  • Reflection: Mentors improve by setting their own standards.
